title: Redis correctness: persistence, atomic work, and lock expiry
outcome: Explain pipeline versus transaction/script, persistence loss windows, and why a lease needs stale-writer protection.
useCase: Distributed workers, counters, and critical lock-based coordination.
benefits: Prevents overclaiming what a fast coordination tool guarantees.
drawbacks: Strong correctness can require authority-side mechanisms beyond Redis.
version: Pinned local examples · version-labelled configuration fragments
cue: Atomic here is not atomic everywhere. A lease can expire.

trace.title: Command boundary
trace.detail: A pipeline batches network operations for efficiency; it does not by itself make them one indivisible business operation. MULTI/EXEC and scripts provide different atomic-execution tools, but Redis transactions do not behave like a relational transaction with automatic rollback of every runtime error.

trace.title: Follow one item
trace.detail:
Trace acquire → pause → expiry → new owner → old owner resumes. Identify which downstream store can reject the old write. Then trace a Redis crash and ask what persisted/replicated data is actually recoverable.

Test the failure model in the isolated lab. Measure the selected durability policy’s behavior, and document what data can be rebuilt versus what needs reconciliation.

trace.title: Try the failure
trace.detail: Atomic commands do not make external effects atomic. Pipeline success is not a database commit. A lock release can delete another owner’s lock if token ownership is not checked.
